newsitem.title: UK: S&P sees more "slow restructuring" of French banks.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees more "slow restructuring" of French banks.

text.p: Standard & Poors said on Monday it sees "further slow restructuring" of the French banking industry for the rest of 1997, after 1996 failed to live up to its initial promise.

S&P said the numerous operations undertaken in 1996, including the acquisition of Banque Francaise du Commerce Exterieur by Credit National, and that of Banque Indosuez by Credit Agricole, but argue that these deals remained "limited in scope," with nothing comparable to the megamerger announced by the insurance companies AXA and UAP.

In a recent report S&P analysts also underlined the fumbled attempt to privatise one of the country's 10 largest retail banks, CIC; the question marks surrounding the future of the quasi-state Credit Foncier de France ; and the "continuing difficulties" that beset the recovery of Credit Lyonnais.

"The French banking system in general, along with Italy's, "remains one of the least profitable in continental Europe, and its performance is well behind that of the banking systems in UK and the U.S.'," S&P said in a statement.

S&P said 16 out of 70 rated banks and financial groups in France had their ratings lowered or placed on CreditWatch negative in 1996. This compared with just six whose ratings were raised or placed on CreditWatch positive.
The agency said in the midst of continued slow restructuring, its analysts believed that a number of "sacred cows" of French banking may be called into question in 1997.
"These might include the special status of the savings banks, the 1937 decree that limits bank opening hours, and the ban on paying interest on sight deposits," S&P said.
"But the biggest challenge facing French banks will be the introduction of the euro."
S&P analysts said in 1997 "French banks will have to think seriously about the challenge posed by a unified market for banking services."
They said not only would the move to the new currency involve high technological costs, but it also spells an end to some forex and cross-border money transfer business.
"European integration will mean further deregulation and heightened competition, with the arrival of institutions that are more efficient and better capitalized than French ones," S&P analysts said.
